Although its fun, its really hard to use, at least for me. This really isnt the type of sandbox game i like, i thought it would be easier to throw a planet into another one, but i had to go through the tutorial twice. i wish it just had some more content as well. if you are a big fan of space, this is the perfect game for you.

I wanted to use Universe Sandbox to visualise everything I've been worldbuilding for a novel. I have done all the extensive calculations to know everything works, but wanted to actually see it.

Universe Sanbox is cool, however, it is extremely fiddly. Planets and moons you add want to "fly by" the suns/planets they're supposed to orbit instead of actually orbiting them.

What made me really give up is when I added a gas giant around a star, and then two Earth-like moons around the giant. On paper, this is a stable setup. The gas giant correctly orbited the star until the two moons were added, at which point nothing I did got it to work. The "auto orbit" button ended up causing more problems, thinking the giant and closest moon were a binary pair.

If you are okay with spending an hour just to add a planet and a couple moons, then go ahead. I personally was not a fan of all the troubleshooting.

It is also worth noting that I have closer to 3 hours at the time of review. The remaining time did not count due to the sandbox crashing.

Universe Sandbox is a simulation game that lets you make all kinds of  experiments. You can create a solar system from scratch or launch a moon at earth at light speed. It offers great complexity, which is super fun for people who are into space.

The graphics look great, the performance is decent. Naturally, the more objects you have in your simulation, the lower your frame rate becomes. The simulation speed also plays a huge role in overall performance. There's not much else to say about visuals. Saturn is missing its famous hexagon, which is interesting.

The soundtrack is very calming and, at times, almost therapeutic. Watching gravity do its work and seeing planets collide or explode never gets old.

If you're into space or simulation games, this game might be for you. If you enjoy both, you'll love it, especially with all the community projects available to browse.

Really fun game to learn more about astronomy and the universe. You can do many fun experiments like establishing a breathable atmosphere on Mars, or making a solar system orbiting a massive red giant star, such as UY Scuti, or even orbiting a black hole. Everything from launching planets into one another, or crashing entire galaxies into eachother is possible. I can wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone interested in space or astrophysics.

10/10

cohorts.label: 100h+
cohorts.summary: Long-term players continue experimenting with celestial mechanics and terraforming despite occasional bugs and crashes.

claims.claim: Reviewers report occasional bugs or crashes, including specific issues with the planet-landing feature and save settings.

citations.review_text:
Despite the fact that this game has been in early access for a really long while, it's a great game. I'm in the process of planning out a stellar network for a game in this, and the amount of customizability in addition to the realism of this makes this a cool game.
At some point I ran into a glitch that kind of messed with my plans ("Pulled by others" and "Pull others" settings didn't persist between saves), the developer got back to that fairly quickly, and it was patched, so now I can continue with my star system design. I hope this game gets more updates in the future and comes out of early access, because oh boy I can only imagine the amount of ideas that can branch from a fully constructed game.
If there's one thing I would like to suggest adding to this game that isn't mentioned on the roadmap it's to add an option to increase UI numeric precision, because sometimes I like working with more precision visible to allow finer tuning of things or seeing subtle changes in mass from various things.
If you're into universe simulators, this is a great one to try out, as long as your PC can handle it.

(also I have the idea that stars with negative luminosity are "anti-matter stars" so I decided to make a binary white dwarf system with that, where one is normal and the other is an exact copy but with negative luminosity. It's just a fun thing I wanted to mention)
